What you make or keep will give you something to look at, and looking at it is what feeds this back. This doesn't need a plan. It needs one thing done today.
3.sheetLine: You kept the role and set down the hands.

4.tense: You are already looking after something specific, and you are talking about it as if it were happening on its own.
4.verb: tending what is growing with steady, responsible care
4.place: the room where what you already are comes out from hiding
4.ask: Name one thing you look after every week and call it yours in that sentence. Out loud, to someone, if someone's there.
4.core:
You water it, you check it, you make the small calls nobody sees, and you describe that work as the situation requiring it or as the job. That work is yours and it's running under your name.

What hasn't been said is that you did it. Asking for credit isn't the move. The move is saying what you did and letting it be seen, because a hand that stays anonymous starts to feel like the work was somebody else's, and that eats at the care itself. Let a piece of this finish, even a small piece. When it does, say so. That isn't fishing for praise. It's admitting you were the one doing it.
4.sheetLine: This work is yours. You keep introducing it as nobody's.

1.tense: Right now you are holding two demands at once and neither one drops.
1.verb: Tending what grows with responsible care
1.place: Standing far enough back to see the whole shape while still inside it
1.ask: Pick one thing you keep going. Say out loud what it has taken from you, then let someone thank you without waving it off. Close the day there.
1.core:
You can carry two demands at once without either one slipping. The bill and the person, the work and the rest — you do not treat them as a coin flip. Both get fed, and from outside it looks easy, though it has not been. That is the whole skill, and it is working on ordinary days, not just the hard ones.

What you have been growing is starting to hold its own weight. You can see the shape of it now, and that also means you can see what it took to get here. Letting a thing be finished does not lose it. You set it down and you still have it.
1.sheetLine: You hold both demands at once, and neither drops.

2.tense: You are already living in a season that has not arrived yet, and steering by it.
2.verb: Tending what grows with responsible care
2.place: Standing far enough back to see the whole shape while still inside it
2.ask: Write down the three outcomes you are most braced for, seal them, and shelve them for a month. Spend the freed attention on one thing that is true this week.
2.core:
Your care is aimed past today. You have the finish mapped before the road shows up, and you are steering toward a version of this you already decided on. Attention that far forward turns into grip, and the grip wears you down.

What it looks like going well is quieter. Something goes in the ground, water gets given, and you let the waiting do its work. Some weeks you can do that, and those weeks hold up. The grip is the thing that is costing you the day in front of you. Tend only this week. What you built last season is not falling apart while you look at it.
2.sheetLine: You are bracing for next year before this week lands.

3.tense: You stopped bringing your care forward, and you are still standing at that door.
3.verb: Tending what grows with responsible care
3.place: Standing far enough back to see the whole shape while still inside it
3.ask: Name one thing you have kept going and one person who knows about it. Tell them plainly that it was hard. Then start something small this week and let them see it.
3.core:
You can still see what needs tending. The stepping forward has gone quiet. You watch the things that want care and do not move toward them — you notice, and your hands stay still. A pattern you used to read at a glance now sits unread.

What looks right here is small and plain: you water one plant badly where someone can see, and it survives. You do not have to start big, and you do not have to feel ready. Pick one thing with a person already in it beside you, and let that be enough for the week. The charge comes back through doing, not through waiting for it.
3.sheetLine: You still see what needs tending — you have stopped reaching.

4.tense: You are holding this together right now, and you describe it like weather.
4.verb: Tending what grows with responsible care
4.place: Standing far enough back to see the whole shape while still inside it
4.ask: When someone asks how it is going, say what you kept going instead of 'fine.' One sentence. Let it land before you move on.
4.core:
You can see the whole shape of this — what is feeding what, what will starve if you look away. You act on that read while you are inside it, and you talk about the results as though they arrived on their own. The work is running. Your name is not on it.

What it looks like going well: you stand back, see the pattern, and say plainly what you did in it. Not the story, not the lesson, just the fact of what you held while things moved. Say it once to one person. Then let something be finished and set it down, because putting down what is done is not losing it.
4.sheetLine: You hold it together, then talk like it happened on its own.

1.tense: You are tending what you are growing and you are letting it finish.
1.verb: tending what is growing with care and a firm hand
1.place: at the point where the work is complete and it's time to let it go
1.ask: Pick one thing you've been holding up and let it stand on its own for a week. Watch what still gets done without your hand on it.
1.core:
You hold the shape of a thing and you don't rush it, and when it's done you step back without making a scene of it. That's not force and it's not doing nothing. Two demands sit in one pair of hands without either getting dropped.

Stepping back reads as natural here because you stayed with it from the start. What you make grows because you sat through the boring middle with it, not because you pushed. There's a next thing this ease is free to feed, if you want it — an invitation, not a bill. The finish is honest, and the work is standing on its own.
1.sheetLine: You hold it well and you let it finish without a fight.

2.tense: You are bracing for a future where the growth will need you on alert.
2.verb: tending what is growing with care and a firm hand
2.place: at the point where the work is complete and it's time to let it go
2.ask: Leave one piece of the work unfinished at the end of the day and walk away from it. Let it rest overnight without checking.
2.core:
You're already managing the next stage before this one is done. There's a future where it all goes wrong, and you're tending that one from here — checking on things, keeping the shape, making sure nothing slips.

What you guard so closely gets crowded. When your hands close in, the space a growing thing needs to keep growing closes too. Two demands held that hard stop being two demands and start being one long squeeze. The finish line keeps moving because you keep moving it.

Leaving it alone overnight won't end it. If one night goes sideways, you'll still be here in the morning, and you'll still know what to do. Let the work survive a few hours without you.
2.sheetLine: You're guarding a future that hasn't asked for you yet.

3.tense: You stopped tending the growing thing at some point behind you, and the door is already shut.
3.verb: tending what is growing with care and a firm hand
3.place: at the point where the work is complete and it's time to let it go
3.ask: Pick one thing you've let sit and put ten minutes of care into it this week. Nothing more. See how your hands feel back on it.
3.core:
There's something you were cultivating, and the care stopped. You know how to do it. You know what it needs. What fell away was the part where you show up and put your hands on it — and the thing is still sitting there, still unfinished, still yours if you want it.

Showing up and getting little back is a hard trade, and at some point the trade stopped being worth it in your hands. The finish didn't get its moment, so the thing stayed where you left it, and you stayed where you were.

You don't have to restart the whole project. Ten minutes on one thing you've been leaving alone. When something reaches its end in your hands, you'll be there for it. You can hand over what you stayed with long enough to see through.
3.sheetLine: You stopped tending something behind you, and it's still there.

4.tense: You are already tending what is growing, but you call it something else.
4.verb: tending what is growing with care and a firm hand
4.place: at the point where the work is complete and it's time to let it go
4.ask: Say out loud one thing you're growing and one thing you do to tend it, without hedging. Do it once this week, to anyone or no one.
4.core:
You shape what grows — the steady care, the calls about what to keep and what to cut, the patience to stay with something through the slow parts. But when it comes up, you describe it as maintenance. The schedule. The obligations. The way things run.

Stewardship is operating through you, and it's costing you energy, and your name isn't on it. You decide what gets cultivated and what gets released, and you call it just what needs doing. The pattern works in the background while you stay the person who keeps the lights on.

Nothing is wrong with the care itself. The only thing missing is the acknowledgment — yours, first, of what you've actually been doing all this time.
4.sheetLine: You're already growing it. You just call it maintenance.
